stem.en: Quick recall before we start: a hockey puck glides across a perfectly frictionless surface at a constant velocity. What is the net force acting on it?

text.en: Zero — Newton's first law says a constant velocity means the net force is zero.

feedback.en: Right, and hold onto this — the second law we're about to meet is really about what happens the moment that net force stops being zero.

text.en: A small constant force in the direction of motion, needed to keep it going.

feedback.en: This is the 'motion needs a force to continue' misconception the first law directly rules out. Constant velocity needs no force at all to sustain it — only a CHANGE in velocity needs one.

text.en: A force equal to the puck's weight.

feedback.en: Weight is one specific force (gravity, pulling down); it's balanced by the ice pushing up, and neither has anything to do with the puck's constant horizontal velocity.

explanation.en: This is the boundary this lesson sits right on: Newton's first law describes what happens when the net force IS zero (nothing changes); Newton's second law, coming up now, describes exactly what happens the instant it isn't.

hints.en: What did Newton's first law say happens to an object's velocity when the net force on it is zero?
Constant velocity — unchanging in speed and direction — is the signature of zero net force.
